performers: Philadelphia Orchestra, Leopold Stokowski (Stokowski’s own orchestration)
intro: Stokowski arranged the organ Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565, for a large orchestra with six horns, four trumpets and four trombones. This is the opening disc side of his 1927 recording with the Philadelphia Orchestra.

sections.label: Intro · Opening D minor flourish
sections.mNote: The organ’s octave gestures are scored as orchestral phrases.

sections.label: A · Toccata runs and held chords
sections.mNote: Fast runs alternate with sustained chords.

sections.label: B · Toccata, closing flourishes
sections.mNote: The free opening moves towards its cadence in D minor.

sections.label: C · Fugue, running subject
sections.mNote: The subject passes through the orchestral parts.

cues.title: Stokowski’s orchestration of the opening
cues.text: The opening flourishes and pauses were written for a single organist. Stokowski spreads them across an orchestra with a large brass section, two harps and celesta.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s Los Angeles Philharmonic note gives the instrumentation of Stokowski’s transcription. https://www.laphil.com/works/toccata-and-fugue-in-d-minor-bwv-565-bach-arr-stokowski
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Recording, Philadelphia, April 1927
cues.text: On 6 April 1927 Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra recorded the work at the Academy of Music. The orchestration was Stokowski’s own. This side holds the opening portion of the recording.
cues.evidence: Swiss Foundation Public Domain transfer, recording metadata: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PDP-CH_-_Philadelphia_Orchestra,_Leopold_Stokowski_-_Toccata_and_Fugue_in_D_minor,_BWV_565_-_Bach_-_Hmv-d1428-5-0761.flac. The orchestration is identified in the LA Phil programme note.

cues.title: Runs over held pedal notes
cues.text: The toccata alternates quick runs with chords. In the organ score, long pedal notes sound beneath the hands. Stokowski keeps this contrast between moving notes and sustained bass in his orchestral transcription.
cues.evidence: BWV 565, toccata: free figuration over held pedal notes, described by the Netherlands Bach Society, https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-565. The LA Phil note identifies the orchestral transcription.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Repertoire for Fantasia, 1938
cues.text: In 1938 Stokowski and Walt Disney discussed music for Fantasia. Stokowski favoured Bach’s “Little” Fugue in G minor, and Disney wanted the Toccata and Fugue. Disney’s choice was adopted, and this orchestration was used in the film.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard, Los Angeles Philharmonic programme note, recounts the 1938 choice of repertoire. https://www.laphil.com/works/toccata-and-fugue-in-d-minor-bwv-565-bach-arr-stokowski

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
